paragraphs: Removing information from a trained model becomes harder when the original training examples are unavailable. This paper develops a certified unlearning framework for that situation. Its aim is to remove the influence of targeted data while preserving the model’s usefulness, without requiring access to the source training samples.

The approach uses a surrogate dataset that approximates the statistical properties of the original data. The statistical distance between these datasets determines how the method scales noise. This connects the unlearning procedure to the quality of the substitute data: the framework explicitly accounts for a mismatch between the surrogate and the source.

The authors establish theoretical bounds, develop practical noise calibration techniques, and evaluate the method on synthetic and real datasets. A central qualification concerns the statistical distance: the theoretical guarantees assume its exact value is known, whereas practical implementations approximate it. Those approximations can weaken the privacy guarantees. The reported experiments support the approach’s effectiveness, while this distinction explains why its formal and practical assurances need to be interpreted separately.
icml-2025-a-certified-unlearning-approac.tldr: A certified unlearning framework uses surrogate data and calibrated noise to remove information when original training samples are unavailable.

paragraphs: Sequence models are increasingly used to learn from graphs, extending architectures designed for ordered inputs to data organized by connections. The paper asks how to compare these choices systematically. Different sequence backbones offer different combinations of efficiency, representational power, and ability to capture distant relationships, making a shared framework useful.

The authors introduce the Graph Sequence Model framework, or GSM, to describe how sequence models operate on graph data. It provides a common basis for examining and comparing the power of different backbones on graph tasks. This makes architectural choices easier to study within one mathematical description.

Using insights from that framework, the authors build GSM++, a fast hybrid model. It first organizes a graph into hierarchical tokens using Hierarchical Affinity Clustering, then processes the resulting sequences with a hybrid architecture. The paper combines theoretical analysis with experiments and reports that GSM++ beats baseline models on most benchmarks. The contribution therefore links a general framework for understanding graph sequence models with a concrete architecture whose reported gains cover most, rather than all, evaluated benchmarks.
icml-2025-best-of-both-worlds-advantages.tldr: A unified framework for graph sequence models motivates GSM++, a hierarchical hybrid architecture that outperforms baselines on most evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Matching markets become harder to coordinate when participants must learn the rewards of possible matches through experience. This paper studies uncertainty on both sides of a market, extending work that mainly considered uncertainty on only one side. The goal is to learn while achieving matchings that are stable under the true rewards.

The authors use the notion of super-stability to handle incomplete information. They show an advantage of Extended Gale-Shapley over standard Gale-Shapley in finding truly stable matchings in this setting. Their centralized learning algorithm achieves logarithmic pessimal stable regret, with its guarantee depending on an instance-specific admissible gap parameter. A decentralized adaptation incurs only a constant additional regret.

The paper also establishes a centralized, instance-dependent lower bound for binary stable regret. This complements the algorithmic guarantee by identifying constraints on what learning can achieve under that measure. Together, the results clarify how the admissible gap and the availability of super-stable matchings help characterize difficulty. The guarantees therefore connect performance to the structure of the particular market, rather than treating all uncertain matching problems as equally hard.
icml-2025-competing-bandits-in-matching-.tldr: Super-stability supports matching algorithms with logarithmic regret when both sides must learn rewards, with difficulty characterized by instance-dependent quantities.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups objects using pairwise labels that say whether each pair is similar or dissimilar. A mistake occurs when the grouping disagrees with a label. The classic Pivot algorithm offers a factor-three approximation, but its worst-case analysis cannot be improved beyond that factor without changing the algorithm.

This paper introduces Modified Pivot, which makes local improvements to Pivot’s output. The appeal is that the modification retains efficient implementations in various settings while improving the quality guarantee. The authors prove an approximation factor strictly below three by an absolute positive constant, establishing that the local changes cross Pivot’s theoretical barrier.

Experiments also show fewer disagreements: on average, Modified Pivot makes less than 77% of the mistakes made by Pivot. This empirical comparison is separate from the worst-case approximation guarantee. For dynamically changing inputs, the paper obtains a better-than-three approximation with polylogarithmic update time. The results matter because they combine an improved provable bound with a modification designed to preserve Pivot’s practical implementation advantages across several computational settings.
icml-2025-correlation-clustering-beyond-.tldr: Modified Pivot improves correlation clustering through local changes, achieving a provable approximation below three and fewer mistakes in experiments.

paragraphs: Counting occurrences in a sequence seems simple, yet it exposes important choices in transformer design. This paper studies small transformer blocks on the histogram task to understand how vocabulary size, embedding size, token mixing, and feed-forward capacity shape the solutions a model can learn. The focus is on how architectural components share the work.

The authors identify two theoretical strategies, called relation-based and inventory-based counting. These define distinct learning regimes and distribute functionality differently between attention and feed-forward layers. Their analysis makes counting a way to examine how the same task can be implemented through different internal arrangements, depending on the available architecture.

The paper also finds that softmax and beginning-of-sequence tokens improve robustness when embedding dimensions are relatively small. Inspection of trained models closely supports the predicted regimes and the emergence of the two strategies during learning. The findings show that even a task built from aggregation and selection can respond strongly to small design changes. They connect observed performance to specific architectural choices and the counting strategies those choices support.
icml-2025-counting-in-small-transformers.tldr: Small transformers learn distinct counting strategies whose success depends on how attention, embeddings, and feed-forward capacity work together.

paragraphs: Training on fewer examples can reduce the data used for learning, but aggressive pruning often harms accuracy. This paper studies whether knowledge distillation helps preserve useful information when training on a subset. Alongside ground-truth labels, the student learns from soft predictions produced by a teacher previously trained on the complete dataset.

The authors give a theoretical motivation for self-distillation and report improvements across the datasets, pruning methods, and pruning fractions they evaluate. A particularly practical finding is that random pruning with distillation performs comparably to, or better than, sophisticated pruning methods across the examined regimes. On ImageNet, they report superior accuracy while training on a random half of the data.

The study also connects the pruning factor with the best weight assigned to distillation, helping address retained examples with noisy labels or poor image quality. Teacher size has a qualified effect: at lower pruning fractions, larger teachers can reduce accuracy, while teachers smaller than the student may help. These findings make the teacher and distillation weight important parts of subset training, alongside the choice of examples.
icml-2025-distilling-the-knowledge-in-da.tldr: Teacher predictions improve training on pruned datasets and can make random subsets competitive with sophisticated selection methods.

paragraphs: How many intermediate reasoning steps does a transformer need to compute a function? This paper connects that question to the Ehrenfeucht-Haussler rank of a Boolean function, a mathematical quantity already important in learning theory. The connection gives an existing complexity measure a direct interpretation in terms of chain-of-thought computation.

The authors prove that the rank equals the minimum number of chain-of-thought steps needed by a single-layer transformer with hard attention. This is an exact characterization within the specified architecture. It therefore identifies both what can be achieved with a given number of steps and when fewer steps cannot suffice.

The characterization yields tight results for particular problems. Composing a function ℓ times requires exactly ℓ reasoning steps, while locating the kth occurrence of 1 in a Boolean sequence requires k steps. These results turn informal questions about reasoning length into precise computational statements. Their scope is the single-layer, hard-attention model studied in the paper, where the rank provides a unified way to express the required amount of intermediate computation.
icml-2025-ehrenfeucht-haussler-rank-and-.tldr: Boolean-function rank exactly characterizes the chain-of-thought steps required by a single-layer hard-attention transformer.

paragraphs: A formally sufficient explanation identifies input features that guarantee a neural network’s prediction remains unchanged. Computing such explanations can require expensive neural network verification. This paper addresses that computational bottleneck with an abstraction-and-refinement method designed to make the verification problem smaller while retaining a guarantee about the original network.

The method constructs a substantially reduced network with a crucial property: an explanation proved sufficient for the reduced model is also sufficient for the original model. Verification can therefore succeed on a smaller object and still establish the desired claim. If the explanation is insufficient for that reduced network, the method gradually increases the network’s size and repeats the process until convergence.

Experiments show improved efficiency in obtaining provably sufficient explanations. The different abstraction levels also provide a finer-grained view of the network’s predictions. The main contribution is the connection between computational simplification and preserved sufficiency: reducing the network creates a faster verification route, and refinement provides a way to add detail when the initial abstraction does not establish the explanation.
icml-2025-explaining-fast-and-slow-abstr.tldr: Reduced network abstractions speed up formally sufficient explanations, with refinement adding detail when the smaller network cannot verify them.

paragraphs: When datasets come from different sources, some features may have changed because of inconsistent measurements, processing, or standardization. Detecting that a distribution changed does not identify which features are responsible. This paper targets that localization problem, which matters when deciding what data to correct or filter before further analysis.

The Feature Shift Localization Network, or FSL-Net, learns from a large collection of datasets. It extracts statistical properties that help it identify shifted features, rather than requiring a new training process for each dataset comparison. The authors describe a network designed to remain fast and accurate on large datasets with many dimensions.

The stated result is that FSL-Net can localize shifts in previously unseen datasets, including shifts it did not encounter during training, without retraining. This makes transfer across datasets central to the approach. Its contribution concerns identifying the features involved in a shift, which can then support investigation of its underlying cause. The authors also provide a trained model and code, making the learned localization procedure available for use.
icml-2025-feature-shift-localization-net.tldr: FSL-Net learns dataset statistics to locate shifted features in large, unseen datasets without retraining.

paragraphs: Grokking describes delayed generalization accompanied by test loss that changes non-monotonically during training. This paper studies the phenomenon in binary logistic classification, a minimal setting where memorizing and generalizing solutions can be defined precisely. The authors find that even this simple model can exhibit grokking near a critical configuration of the problem.

Their analysis uses the implicit bias of gradient descent. Grokking can occur when training data are nearly linearly separable from the origin and noise is strong in perpendicular directions. Near this boundary, some directions in the loss landscape have almost no gradient. Training can consequently spend arbitrarily long periods near quasi-stable solutions before eventually reaching the global minimum.

Empirical observations and analytical results support this mechanism within the studied setting. The authors also connect it to related findings and strengthen the conjecture that grokking generally occurs near the interpolation threshold. That broader connection remains a conjecture. The concrete contribution is an explanation of how very slow movement through nearly flat regions can produce delayed generalization in a simple classification model.
icml-2025-grokking-at-the-edge-of-linear.tldr: Logistic regression can exhibit grokking near a separability boundary, where nearly flat loss directions cause long delays before generalization.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to align two heterogeneous datasets when no correspondences between their points are known. The objective is to place both datasets in a common metric space, giving them a shared representation based on distances. The proposed formulation uses unbalanced optimal transport with Gromov–Wasserstein penalties on its marginals.

The authors establish that their objective has a minimizer. They also characterize its connection to embedded Wasserstein distance: as the penalty parameters grow without bound, the corresponding minimizers converge to a minimizer of that distance. This gives the formulation a precise limiting relationship to another alignment objective and positions it as a counterpart to joint multidimensional scaling.

For computation, the model is rewritten as a quadratic, multi-marginal, unbalanced transport problem. A bi-convex relaxation can then be solved numerically through block-coordinate descent, which updates groups of variables in turn. Numerical examples demonstrate joint embeddings in both Euclidean and non-Euclidean spaces. The work thus combines an existence result and a limiting characterization with a computational route through a relaxed version of the problem.
icml-2025-joint-metric-space-embedding-b.tldr: An optimal-transport formulation aligns datasets without known correspondences, with existence and convergence results plus a solver for a relaxed problem.

paragraphs: Off-policy methods use logged decisions and their outcomes to evaluate or learn a different policy. Each record includes the context, action, feedback, and probability assigned to that action. Estimation becomes difficult when these probabilities are poor quality or rewards have heavy tails, because unusually large contributions can create high variance.

The paper proposes an estimator built from the log-sum-exponential operator. The authors report reduced variance and robustness to heavy-tailed conditions compared with traditional inverse propensity score estimators. For evaluation, they derive upper bounds on both bias and variance, explicitly accounting for two sources of estimation error.

For policy learning, they bound regret under the assumption that the weighted reward has a bounded moment of order 1+ε. The stated rate is O(n^(−ε/(1+ε))) for ε between zero and one, where n is the logged dataset size. Thus, the bound’s rate depends on the moment assumption. Empirical evaluations in both learning and evaluation support practical advantages, complementing the theoretical account of how the estimator behaves under difficult reward distributions.
icml-2025-log-sum-exponential-estimator-.tldr: A log-sum-exponential estimator improves off-policy estimation robustness, with bias, variance, and moment-dependent regret bounds.

paragraphs: Intermediate scratchpad steps can expand the computational capabilities of transformers, but expressivity alone does not say how long a scratchpad must be. This paper investigates that length requirement. It focuses on lower bounds: statements showing that a model needs at least a certain number of chain-of-thought steps to solve a problem.

The motivation comes from a gap between broad theoretical capability and observed reasoning requirements. Polynomial-length scratchpads can extend expressivity from TC⁰ to PTIME, yet empirical evidence suggests that transformers also need scratchpads for some problems already in TC⁰, including parity and multiplication. Circuit-complexity classifications therefore leave important questions about the amount of intermediate computation unresolved.

The authors systematically study several algorithmic problems in the hard-attention setting and obtain bounds that are tight up to logarithmic factors. This qualification means the characterization retains a logarithmic gap rather than giving an exact step count. The results contribute a more detailed picture of chain-of-thought’s computational cost, identifying limits on how short reasoning sequences can be within the transformer regime under study.
icml-2025-lower-bounds-for-chain-of-thou.tldr: The paper establishes near-tight lower bounds on chain-of-thought length for algorithmic problems in hard-attention transformers.

paragraphs: Conformal regression produces prediction intervals, but their usefulness depends on their length as well as their coverage. This paper studies how close split conformal intervals come to the shortest oracle interval. It treats the difference in length as excess volume loss, making interval efficiency the central quantity of interest.

The authors interpret calibration as an empirical volume-minimization problem and derive a finite-sample upper bound on excess volume loss for classical split conformal regression. They then introduce EffOrt, which changes the learning stage so that the base prediction function is chosen with the final interval length in mind. The analysis connects predictor learning with the later calibration step.

That connection reveals how the choice of predictor function class affects the resulting interval efficiency. The authors also propose Ad-EffOrt, which allows interval sizes to vary with the covariates, and evaluate the methods’ empirical performance and robustness. The contribution is a framework for studying and improving interval length across both learning and calibration, rather than treating the predictor as unrelated to the size of the eventual uncertainty interval.
icml-2025-on-volume-minimization-in-conf.tldr: EffOrt selects predictors to reduce conformal interval length, supported by excess-volume bounds and an extension with input-dependent interval sizes.

paragraphs: Quantum error mitigation aims to make results from noisy quantum devices more reliable. Machine learning approaches have shown promise, but comparisons across studies are difficult when datasets and experimental settings differ. This paper addresses that evaluation problem by introducing QEM-Bench, a shared benchmark for learning-based quantum error mitigation.

The benchmark contains twenty-two datasets spanning different circuit types and noise profiles. That variety gives researchers a common setting in which to compare methods across multiple kinds of quantum computations and noise. The paper also introduces QEMFormer, a refined learning pipeline that serves as a baseline within this evaluation framework.

QEMFormer combines a feature encoder that preserves local, global, and topological circuit information with a two-branch model for short-range and long-range dependencies. The design brings several views of circuit structure into the mitigation process. Experiments on QEM-Bench show better performance than the existing baselines evaluated. Together, the benchmark and model contribute both a more consistent basis for comparison and evidence that integrating information across circuit scales can improve learning-based mitigation.
icml-2025-qem-bench-benchmarking-learnin.tldr: QEM-Bench standardizes quantum error mitigation evaluation, and QEMFormer improves benchmark performance by combining circuit information across multiple scales.

paragraphs: Conformal outlier detection uses a reference set of normal examples to calibrate false-alarm control. In practice, some supposed normal examples may actually be outliers. This paper studies what happens under that contamination, focusing on both type-I error, which concerns falsely flagging normal data, and power, the ability to detect outliers.

The authors prove that contamination yields conservative type-I error control under realistic, non-adversarial conditions. The method can therefore remain cautious about false alarms, but that conservativeness typically reduces detection power. This explains how contamination can make a detector less useful even when it does not invalidate false-alarm control.

To recover power, the paper proposes active cleaning with a limited labeling budget. An outlier model selects suspicious reference points for annotation, and only confirmed outliers among those points are removed. Theoretical analysis supports this selective strategy’s ability to improve power while mitigating the risk of inflated type-I error. Experiments on real datasets show the predicted conservative behavior and report improved power without loss of validity after cleaning.
icml-2025-robust-conformal-outlier-detec.tldr: Under non-adversarial conditions, contaminated conformal reference data produce conservative detection, and targeted labeling can recover power while preserving validity.

paragraphs: Long-context transformers retain a key-value cache so they can reuse information during decoding. That cache grows with input length, increasing memory capacity and bandwidth demands. RocketKV addresses these costs through a training-free compression method that combines permanent cache reduction with finer selection during attention.

The first stage evicts cached information for input tokens at a coarse level. The second stage applies hybrid sparse attention, selecting a top-k set using approximate attention scores. Those approximations reduce both head and sequence dimensions. The two stages therefore address different parts of the problem: how much information remains cached and how much of it attention uses.

Compared with a full-cache baseline on an NVIDIA A100, the paper reports up to 400-fold compression, up to 3.7-fold end-to-end speedup, and up to 32.6% lower peak memory during decoding, with negligible accuracy loss across varied long-context tasks. These are reported maxima. A multi-turn variant also consistently outperforms the compared methods and approaches oracle top-k attention accuracy, supporting the approach’s usefulness beyond a single interaction.
icml-2025-rocketkv-accelerating-long-con.tldr: RocketKV combines cache eviction and sparse attention to accelerate long-context inference with negligible accuracy loss in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Latent stochastic differential equations model time series and sequences through hidden dynamics that include randomness. Training them commonly uses adjoint sensitivity methods, which depend on simulating approximate trajectories and propagating learning signals through those solutions. This numerical work creates a scalability bottleneck for an otherwise useful class of models.

The paper introduces SDE Matching, a training method that avoids those simulations. Its design draws on score matching and flow matching, approaches used to learn generative dynamics, and extends their ideas to stochastic dynamics for time series. The key change is in how the latent dynamics are learned: training no longer requires the costly numerical simulations used by the conventional approach.

The reported results show performance comparable to adjoint sensitivity methods while substantially reducing computational complexity. The contribution is therefore an alternative training route that retains the usefulness demonstrated by the existing approach in the reported results. By addressing the simulation-dependent training bottleneck directly, SDE Matching makes scalability a property of the learning procedure rather than requiring the time-series modeling task itself to change.
icml-2025-sde-matching-scalable-and-simu.tldr: SDE Matching trains latent stochastic differential equations without numerical simulation, reporting comparable performance with substantially lower computational complexity.

paragraphs: Dyna-style reinforcement learning supplements collected experience with synthetic state transitions generated by a model. The intended benefit is better use of real interaction data. This paper investigates why that approach performs unevenly across control benchmarks whose observations describe the agent’s own physical state.

The authors find a substantial contrast between OpenAI Gym and the DeepMind Control Suite. Dyna-style methods perform well on Gym control tasks but can lose considerable performance on similar tasks in the Control Suite, despite the two settings using identical physics backends. The comparison shows that similarity in task description and physics does not ensure that synthetic experience will provide the same training benefit.

Techniques intended to address several relevant problems do not consistently improve results across environments. More directly, adding synthetic rollouts significantly reduces performance in most of the evaluated Control Suite environments. The finding concerns the central mechanism of Dyna-style learning, not just an incidental implementation choice. It supports evaluating model-generated training data across diverse settings before assuming that its sample-efficiency benefits will transfer.
icml-2025-stealing-that-free-lunch-expos.tldr: Synthetic rollouts that help Dyna-style reinforcement learning on Gym can significantly degrade performance across most evaluated DeepMind Control Suite environments.

paragraphs: A graph representation should remain unchanged when its nodes are renamed, while still capturing useful structural differences. This paper develops a family of graph embeddings with that invariance property. It generalizes the existing Skew Spectrum using group theory and harmonic analysis to cover a wider range of graph structures.

The extension handles attributed graphs, multilayer graphs, and hypergraphs, which the original Skew Spectrum could not represent in this way. It also defines a family of functions that offers choices between computational cost and expressivity. This makes the representation adaptable to how much computation is available and how much structural information needs to be distinguished.

The authors formally prove invariance and demonstrate improved expressiveness experimentally. They also apply generalization-preserving heuristics to improve expressivity at the same computational cost as the original Skew Spectrum, and discuss efficient computation. The result combines a wider domain of supported structures with a flexible computational tradeoff. Its formal guarantee concerns invariance to graph isomorphism, while the reported experiments provide evidence for the improvement in expressive power.
icml-2025-the-generalized-skew-spectrum-.tldr: A generalized Skew Spectrum provides invariant embeddings for richer graph types and adjustable tradeoffs between expressivity and computation.

paragraphs: People often predict an agent’s actions by attributing beliefs, intentions, and goals to it. For AI systems, such explanations could help anticipate behavior in situations that are difficult to evaluate comprehensively. This paper asks how reliably beliefs inferred from observed behavior can support predictions in new environments.

The analysis assumes that the agent’s behavior is guided by a world model. Under that assumption, the authors derive bounds on behavior in previously unseen deployment environments. These bounds provide a theoretical account of the limits of predicting intentional agents using behavioral data alone, connecting observations in one setting to what can be inferred about another.

The significance lies in giving a precise mathematical treatment to a common explanatory practice. An inferred belief or goal is useful for prediction only to the extent that the available behavioral evidence supports its implications in a new setting. The paper’s bounds characterize that issue within its world-model assumption. The authors discuss consequences for safety and fairness, where predictions about unfamiliar deployment conditions can be especially consequential.
icml-2025-the-limits-of-predicting-agent.tldr: Assuming an agent acts through a world model, the paper bounds how well behavioral observations can predict its actions in unseen environments.

paragraphs: Best-of-n alignment generates n candidates from a reference model, scores them with a reward function, and returns the highest-ranked candidate. This paper examines how that selection changes the output distribution and how often the selected output wins against the reference policy. These quantities describe two sides of the method’s alignment tradeoff.

The authors correct a commonly used claim about KL divergence, a measure of distributional change. The expression log(n) − (n−1)/n is an upper bound on the actual divergence, rather than an exact formula. They study when this bound is tight and propose a new divergence estimator that gives a close approximation in their empirical evaluation.

They also prove that the win rate against the reference policy is at most n/(n+1), with bounds describing the tightness of that characterization. Combining the results, they analyze the balance between improved win rate and departure from the reference distribution. Their analysis indicates that very good tradeoffs are achievable with fewer than one thousand candidates, while preserving the distinction between upper bounds and quantities actually attained.
icml-2025-theoretical-guarantees-on-the-.tldr: The paper corrects an exact-divergence claim for best-of-n alignment and derives bounds describing its win-rate and distribution-shift tradeoff.

paragraphs: Ensembles combine multiple models, but the ease of understanding each component does not by itself explain how hard the combined system is to interpret. This paper studies that question through computational complexity. It examines how the number, size, and type of component models affect the difficulty of generating explanations.

The analysis finds that small components do not necessarily make explanation tractable. Under standard complexity assumptions such as P ≠ NP, explaining ensembles can remain computationally intractable even when each base model has constant size. The number of components and their model family also matter, producing different complexity patterns across ensemble configurations.

A striking contrast concerns ensembles with few members. Small ensembles of decision trees admit efficient interpretation, while ensembles of linear models can remain intractable even with a constant number of components. The contribution is a mathematical account of why ensemble interpretability depends on more than individual model simplicity. It frames interpretation as an explanation-computation problem and identifies configurations where that problem changes sharply in difficulty.
icml-2025-what-makes-an-ensemble-un-inte.tldr: The computational difficulty of explaining ensembles depends jointly on component count, size, and type, with sharply different results for trees and linear models.

paragraphs: When language-model applications spend substantial computation during inference, generation speed becomes especially important. This paper introduces xLSTM 7B, a seven-billion-parameter recurrent language model designed for that setting. It combines the xLSTM architecture with targeted optimizations intended to make inference faster and more efficient at this model scale.

The architectural motivation is that xLSTM offers computation that scales linearly with sequence length and constant memory usage. The paper moves beyond those desirable scaling properties to assess a larger model’s actual performance and inference efficiency. This connects an architectural argument about resource use with measurements of a concrete language model.

The experiments report downstream performance comparable to other similarly sized language models, alongside substantially faster and more efficient inference than the Llama- and Mamba-based models compared. The authors characterize xLSTM 7B as the fastest and most efficient seven-billion-parameter model on the basis of these results. The findings support its potential for applications that rely heavily on inference-time computation. Model weights, model code, and training code are released as open source.
icml-2025-xlstm-7b-a-recurrent-llm-for-f.tldr: xLSTM 7B combines recurrent architecture and inference optimizations, reporting comparable task performance with faster inference than the Llama- and Mamba-based models compared.

paragraphs: Vision-based reinforcement learning agents often struggle when their environment changes. Collecting many task variations or augmenting training images can help, but these approaches add data and computational demands and can complicate training. This paper studies a representation-based approach to generalizing to new task variations without relying on data augmentation.

The proposed model, Associative Latent DisentAnglement, or ALDA, builds on standard off-policy reinforcement learning. Inspired by computational neuroscience, it combines latent disentanglement with a model of associative memory. The central idea is to use these two components together to support transfer, and the authors demonstrate zero-shot generalization on difficult task variations.

The paper also provides a formal result characterizing data augmentation as a weak form of disentanglement. This links a widely used generalization technique to the representation property that motivates ALDA. The empirical and theoretical contributions serve different roles: the model demonstrates generalization without augmentation in the studied variations, while the formal analysis explains a connection between augmentation and disentanglement. Together, they motivate examining learned representations and associative memory as mechanisms for transfer.
icml-2025-zero-shot-generalization-of-vi.tldr: ALDA combines latent disentanglement and associative memory to demonstrate zero-shot visual reinforcement-learning generalization without data augmentation.
